title: Always write units and state symbols
body: in equations. Conditions (temperature, catalyst, solvent) are a **mark** in organic equations: write them over the arrow.

title: Mole bridge
body: Every calculation is: *given $\to$ moles $\to$ ratio from the balanced equation $\to$ moles of wanted $\to$ answer.* Write the mole ratio line explicitly.

title: Number of significant figures
body: match the data (usually 3). Don't round intermediate steps.

title: Command words
body: *State* — one fact; *Explain* — reason with chemistry; *Suggest* — apply knowledge to something new; *Deduce* — reasoned conclusion from information given; *Calculate* — show working with units.

title: Colours and observations
body: give the **initial** and **final** colour ("orange to green") and the **state** (white precipitate, effervescence). "Clear" is not the same as "colourless".

title: Core formulae
body: $n=\dfrac mM$; $n=cV$ with $V$ in $\mathrm{dm}^3$ ($\mathrm{cm}^3\div1000$); gas at r.t.p. $n=\dfrac V{24.0\ \mathrm{dm}^3}$ (r.t.p. $20^\circ\mathrm C$, $1$ atm); $pV=nRT$ in SI units (**Pa, $\mathrm m^3$, K**; $\mathrm{dm}^3\to\mathrm m^3$ is $\times10^{-3}$).

title: Titration
body: $\dfrac{c_1V_1}{n_1}=\dfrac{c_2V_2}{n_2}$ with $n_1,n_2$ the **stoichiometric coefficients** — skips moles altogether. Use **concordant** titres (within $0.10\ \mathrm{cm^3}$) and average them. For a scaled-down aliquot ($25\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ from $250\ \mathrm{cm^3}$) **multiply by 10 at the end**.

title: Empirical formula
body: percentage $\to$ divide by $A_r$ $\to$ divide by the smallest. If a ratio is $x.5$ multiply all by 2; $x.33$ or $x.67$ multiply by 3; $x.25$ or $x.75$ multiply by 4.

title: Molecular formula
body: $\dfrac{M_r}{\text{empirical mass}}=k$, multiply the empirical formula by $k$ (should be a whole number).

title: Limiting reagent
body: divide each reagent's moles by its coefficient; the **smaller** value is limiting. Everything else is in excess.

title: Percentage yield and atom economy
body: yield $=\dfrac{\text{actual}}{\text{theoretical}}\times100$; atom economy $=\dfrac{M_r\text{ of desired product}}{\sum M_r\text{ of all products}}\times100$ (using the balanced equation).

title: Dilution
body: $c_1V_1=c_2V_2$. Serial dilution: multiply dilution factors.

title: Concentration conversion
body: $\mathrm{g\,dm^{-3}}=\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}\times M_r$. Percent by mass, ppm ($\times10^{-6}$).

title: Gas volumes, same $T$ and $p$
body: **volume ratio $=$ mole ratio** (Avogadro). Combustion of a hydrocarbon $\mathrm C_xH_y$: $V_{\mathrm{CO_2}}:V_{\mathrm{O_2\,used}}$ gives $x$ and $y$ directly: $x=\dfrac{V_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{V_{\text{hydrocarbon}}}$, water (liquid) volume change gives $y$.

title: $M_r$ from a gas
body: $M=\dfrac{mRT}{pV}$ (SI units). Density relation $\rho=\dfrac{pM}{RT}$.

title: Combustion analysis
body: $\mathrm{CO_2}\to$ moles of C, $\mathrm{H_2O}\to$ **twice** the moles of H, oxygen by difference.

title: Average $A_r$
body: $\dfrac{\sum(\text{abundance}\times\text{mass})}{\sum\text{abundance}}$; if the abundance is given as relative peak heights, same formula.

title: Number of atoms/ions
body: $N=n\times6.02\times10^{23}$; count ions in the **formula unit** ($\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3}$ has 5 ions).

title: Oxidation numbers
body: free element $0$; group 1 $+1$; group 2 $+2$; F $-1$; H $+1$ (hydrides $-1$); O $-2$ (peroxides $-1$, OF$_2$ $+2$); halogens $-1$ in halides; **sum equals the overall charge**. Redox: the species that gains electrons (oxidation number falls) is reduced and is the **oxidising agent**.

title: Balancing redox quickly
body: change in oxidation number $\times$ number of atoms $=$ electrons; equalise electrons, then O with $\mathrm{H_2O}$, H with $\mathrm H^+$, charge with $e^-$ (acid conditions).

title: Ionic equations
body: write the full equation, split the aqueous ionic compounds, cancel **spectators**.

title: Mass spectrometry
body: **M+1 peak** gives the number of carbons: $\dfrac{\text{M+1 height}}{\text{M height}}\times\dfrac{100}{1.1}=n_C$. Chlorine: $\mathrm{M:M{+}2}=3:1$; bromine $1:1$; $\mathrm{Cl_2}$: $9:6:1$; $\mathrm{Br_2}$: $1:2:1$.

title: Electron configuration
body: fill $1s,2s,2p,3s,3p,4s,3d,4p,5s,4d\dots$; **$4s$ fills first and empties first** when forming ions. Exceptions: **Cr** $[\mathrm{Ar}]3d^54s^1$ and **Cu** $[\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^1$ (half-filled and filled $d$ are stable). Transition-metal ions lose $4s$ then $3d$.

title: Successive ionisation energies identify the group
body: a **big jump** shows the electrons being removed from an inner shell, so the number of electrons before the jump $=$ group number.

title: Ionisation energy trends
body: across a period increases (nuclear charge up, same shielding); down a group decreases (more shells, more shielding). **Dips at the start of $p$ (e.g. Al below Mg, S below P)**: for Al, the electron is in a higher-energy $3p$ subshell; for S, **paired** $3p$ electrons repel. The same logic gives dips at B/O.

title: Isoelectronic species
body: same electrons; the more protons, the smaller the radius ($\mathrm{O^{2-}}>\mathrm{F^-}>\mathrm{Na^+}>\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}>\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$).

title: Shape in seconds (VSEPR)
body:
Count the **electron domains** on the central atom: $\dfrac{\text{valence electrons}+\text{atoms bonded (monovalent)}-\text{charge}}{2}$. Then:

| Domains | Lone pairs | Shape | Bond angle |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 0 | linear | $180^\circ$ |
| 3 | 0 / 1 | trigonal planar / bent | $120^\circ$ / $<120^\circ$ |
| 4 | 0 / 1 / 2 | tetrahedral / pyramidal / bent | $109.5^\circ$ / $107^\circ$ / $104.5^\circ$ |
| 5 | 0 | trigonal bipyramidal | $90^\circ,120^\circ$ |
| 6 | 0 / 2 | octahedral / square planar | $90^\circ$ |

  **Each lone pair squeezes the angle by about $2.5^\circ$** (lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs). Double bonds count as one domain. Common ones: $\mathrm{BF_3}$ trigonal planar, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ linear, $\mathrm{SO_2}$ bent, $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ tetrahedral, $\mathrm{SF_6}$ octahedral, $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ trigonal bipyramidal, $\mathrm{XeF_4}$ square planar.

title: Polarity
body: a molecule with polar bonds is non-polar overall if its **shape is symmetric** ($\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{CCl_4}$, $\mathrm{BF_3}$, $\mathrm{SF_6}$); polar if not ($\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{CHCl_3}$).

title: Sigma and pi counting
body: single bond $=1\sigma$; double $=1\sigma+1\pi$; triple $=1\sigma+2\pi$. Ethene has $5\sigma+1\pi$; benzene has $12\sigma$ and a delocalised $\pi$ system.

title: Intermolecular force ranking
body: (boiling point): hydrogen bonding (**needs H on N, O or F and a lone pair on N, O or F**) $>$ permanent dipole $>$ instantaneous dipole (London) — but **London forces grow with the number of electrons**, so a big non-polar molecule can beat a small polar one.

title: Boiling point reasoning template
body: type of force $\to$ strength $\to$ energy needed to overcome. For ionic or giant covalent say **bonds**, for simple molecules say **intermolecular forces**, never "break covalent bonds" for simple molecular melting.

title: Hydrogen bond count
body: water forms about 2 per molecule; ethanol 1 on average; carboxylic acids dimerise.

title: Ionic radius and lattice energy
body: lattice energy magnitude $\propto\dfrac{|q_+\,q_-|}{r_++r_-}$. $\mathrm{MgO}\gg\mathrm{NaCl}$ because of the $2{+}/2{-}$ charges and small ions.

title: Metallic bonding
body: attraction between cations and delocalised electrons; strength increases with ionic charge and decreasing radius (Mg $>$ Na).

title: Bond energy and length
body: higher order means shorter and stronger. $\mathrm{C{-}C}\,347$, $\mathrm{C{=}C}\,612$, $\mathrm{C{\equiv}C}\,838\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

title: Allotropes
body: graphite conducts (delocalised electrons between layers), diamond doesn't; graphene is a single layer.

title: Ideal gas
body: $pV=nRT$. **Ratio form** for fixed $n$: $\dfrac{p_1V_1}{T_1}=\dfrac{p_2V_2}{T_2}$ (K). Real gases deviate at **high pressure** (molecular volume matters) and **low temperature** (intermolecular forces matter). The closest to ideal: small, non-polar ($\mathrm{He}$, $\mathrm{H_2}$).

title: Dalton's law
body: $p_i=x_iP_{\text{total}}$ where $x_i$ is the mole fraction. Total pressure is the sum of partial pressures.

title: Conversions
body: $1\ \mathrm{atm}=101\ 325\ \mathrm{Pa}$; $1\ \mathrm{dm^3}=10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}$; $T/\mathrm K=\theta/^\circ\mathrm C+273$.

title: Liquid and solid properties
body: giant ionic/covalent/metallic structures — high melting points; simple molecular — low.

title: Lattice types
body: simple cubic, body-centred, face-centred; **ionic conduction needs mobile ions** (molten or aqueous).

title: Sublimation
body: $\mathrm{I_2}$, dry ice, graphite.

title: Bond enthalpy method
body: $\Delta H=\sum(\text{bonds broken})-\sum(\text{bonds formed})$. Count **every** bond of every molecule, including the unchanged bonds only if they change (you can cancel them).

title: Hess's law from formation data
body: $\Delta H_r=\sum\Delta H_f(\text{products})-\sum\Delta H_f(\text{reactants})$ — **elements in standard states have $\Delta H_f=0$**; multiply by the coefficients.

title: Hess's law from combustion data
body: $\Delta H_r=\sum\Delta H_c(\text{reactants})-\sum\Delta H_c(\text{products})$ (the **reverse** order to formation).

title: Cycle direction rule
body: (energy-cycle triangle): $\Delta H$ along a route in the direction of an arrow is positive; against it, negative. If unsure, write $\Delta H_{\text{target}}=\Delta H_1+\Delta H_2$ along the alternative path and reverse the signs of any step taken backwards.

title: Calorimetry
body: $q=mc\Delta T$ with $m$ the mass of **water/solution** (not the solid) and $c=4.18\ \mathrm{J\,g^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ (1 cm³ of dilute solution $\approx1\ \mathrm g$). $\Delta H=-\dfrac q{n}$ ($\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$; **negative for a temperature rise**). Divide by the **limiting** reagent's moles.

title: Calorimetry errors
body: heat loss to surroundings (give a lower $\Delta T$), incomplete combustion, evaporation of the fuel, heat absorbed by the calorimeter. **Use extrapolated cooling curves** for $\Delta T$ at the mixing time.

title: Enthalpy of neutralisation
body: about $-57\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ for strong acid + strong base; weak acids give less (energy needed to ionise).

title: Enthalpy change of solution
body: Cambridge defines lattice energy as the **formation** of the lattice from gaseous ions (negative), so $\Delta H_{\text{sol}}=-\Delta H_{\text{latt}}+\sum\Delta H_{\text{hyd}}$. Draw the cycle (gaseous ions on top, solid and solution below) to check the signs.

title: Born–Haber cycle
body: atomisation, ionisation energy, electron affinity, lattice energy: write the cycle with arrows up for endothermic. $\Delta H_f=\Delta H_{at}(\mathrm M)+\mathrm{IE}+\tfrac12\Delta H_{at}(\mathrm X_2)+\mathrm{EA}+\Delta H_{\text{latt}}$. **Lattice energy is the unknown on the bottom line.**

title: Entropy
body: $\Delta S_{\text{sys}}$ is positive when the number of **gas** moles rises (gas $\gg$ liquid $>$ solid) or a solid dissolves. Standard entropy change $\Delta S^\circ=\sum S^\circ(\text{products})-\sum S^\circ(\text{reactants})$.

title: Gibbs
body: $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S$; **feasible if $\Delta G<0$**. Be careful with units: $\Delta H$ in kJ, $\Delta S$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ (divide by 1000). **Temperature at which a reaction becomes feasible:** $T=\dfrac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}$. Sign table: $(-\Delta H,+\Delta S)$ always feasible; $(+\Delta H,-\Delta S)$ never; the other two depend on $T$.

title: $\Delta G$ links
body: $\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K=-nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}$ (not on the data booklet in that form). $E^\circ>0\Leftrightarrow K>1\Leftrightarrow\Delta G^\circ<0$.

title: Energy level diagrams
body: label reactants, products, $\Delta H$ (vertical arrow) and $E_a$ (from reactants to the top of the hump). Catalysts lower $E_a$ but not $\Delta H$.

title: Mean bond enthalpy limitations
body: gas-phase averages, so answers are approximate vs formation data.

title: Standard conditions
body: $298\ \mathrm K$, $100\ \mathrm{kPa}$ (or 1 bar), $1\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$.

title: Cell potential
body: $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=E^\circ_{\text{(more positive)}}-E^\circ_{\text{(less positive)}}=E^\circ_{\text{reduction}}-E^\circ_{\text{oxidation}}$. The more positive electrode is the **cathode** (reduction); electrons flow from the more negative electrode through the wire.

title: Predicting reactions
body: **anticlockwise rule** — the more negative $E^\circ$ half-equation goes backwards (oxidation); the reaction is feasible if $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}>0$. Feasible does **not** mean fast (kinetics).

title: Electrolysis amounts
body: $Q=It$, moles of electrons $=\dfrac Q F$ ($F=96\ 500\ \mathrm{C\,mol^{-1}}$), then use the half-equation ratio. Mass $=\dfrac{ItM}{zF}$. **Metal ion charge $z$ equals electrons per atom.** Same current in series: moles of product proportional to $\dfrac1z$.

title: Electrolysis products
body: at the **cathode** the less reactive species gets reduced ($\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ before $\mathrm{H^+}$; $\mathrm H_2$ over $\mathrm{Na^+}$); at the **anode**, halide before water unless dilute (concentrated $\mathrm{NaCl}$ gives $\mathrm{Cl_2}$; dilute gives $\mathrm{O_2}$). Mnemonic: **AN OX, RED CAT**.

title: Nernst (A Level)
body: $E=E^\circ+\dfrac{0.059}{z}\lg\dfrac{[\mathrm{ox}]}{[\mathrm{red}]}$ at $298\ \mathrm K$. **A tenfold increase in the oxidised ion changes $E$ by $0.059/z\ \mathrm V$** (less for larger $z$).

title: Standard hydrogen electrode
body: $1\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}\ \mathrm H^+$, $100\ \mathrm{kPa}$ $\mathrm H_2$, $298\ \mathrm K$, platinum electrode coated in platinum black.

title: Salt bridge
body: completes the circuit by ion flow without mixing; must not react with the ions ($\mathrm{KNO_3}$ not $\mathrm{KCl}$ with $\mathrm{Ag^+}$).

title: Fuel cell, batteries
body: the hydrogen–oxygen cell: negative $\mathrm H_2+2\mathrm{OH^-}\to2\mathrm{H_2O}+2e^-$; positive $\mathrm O_2+2\mathrm{H_2O}+4e^-\to4\mathrm{OH^-}$ (alkaline).

title: Titration data and $E^\circ$
body: $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ is a strong oxidiser, so **no indicator** (self-indicating pink). Don't acidify with HCl (the chloride is oxidised) — use $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$.

title: $K_c$ and $K_p$
body: products over reactants raised to powers; **omit solids and pure liquids**. $K_p$ uses partial pressures $p_i=x_iP$. $K_p=K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}$ where $\Delta n=\sum\text{gas products}-\sum\text{gas reactants}$ (not on the data booklet).

title: Units of $K$
body: compute them, don't guess: $K_c$ for $\mathrm A+\mathrm B\rightleftharpoons\mathrm C$ has $\mathrm{mol^{-1}\,dm^3}$. $\Delta n=0\Rightarrow$ no units.

title: ICE tables
body: **I**nitial, **C**hange (use the stoichiometric ratio), **E**quilibrium. Fill in the known equilibrium amount first and work back.

title: Le Chatelier shortcut
body: the system shifts to oppose the change. Pressure up favours **fewer gas moles**; temperature up favours the **endothermic** direction; **only temperature changes the value of $K$**; a catalyst doesn't shift the equilibrium, only the speed.

title: Reaction quotient $Q$
body: $Q<K$ moves forward, $Q>K$ moves back.

title: pH of a strong acid
body: $\mathrm{pH}=-\lg[\mathrm H^+]$ ($[\mathrm H^+]=c$ for monoprotic, $2c$ for diprotic). **Strong base:** $[\mathrm H^+]=\dfrac{K_w}{[\mathrm{OH^-}]}$ with $K_w=1.0\times10^{-14}$; $\mathrm{pH}=14-\mathrm{pOH}$. **A tenfold dilution raises the pH of a strong acid by $1$.**

title: pH of a weak acid (the approximation)
body: $[\mathrm H^+]=\sqrt{K_ac}$, so $\mathrm{pH}=\tfrac12\left(\mathrm pK_a-\lg c\right)$. Valid when ionisation is small (check $[\mathrm H^+]\ll c$). **Weak base:** $[\mathrm{OH^-}]=\sqrt{K_bc}$. $\mathrm pK_a+\mathrm pK_b=14$ for a conjugate pair.

title: Buffers (Henderson–Hasselbalch)
body: $\mathrm{pH}=\mathrm pK_a+\lg\dfrac{[\mathrm A^-]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}$ (not on the data booklet). **At half-neutralisation $[\mathrm A^-]=[\mathrm{HA}]$ so $\mathrm{pH}=\mathrm pK_a$.** Making a buffer: weak acid + its salt, or **excess** weak acid + some strong base (moles after reaction, not initial).

title: How a buffer works
body: added $\mathrm H^+$ is removed by $\mathrm A^-$ ($\mathrm A^-+\mathrm H^+\to\mathrm{HA}$); added $\mathrm{OH^-}$ by $\mathrm{HA}$ ($\mathrm{HA}+\mathrm{OH^-}\to\mathrm A^-+\mathrm{H_2O}$). **Both** components must be present in large amounts. Capacity is greatest when $[\mathrm A^-]=[\mathrm{HA}]$.

title: Indicator choice for a titration
body: pick one whose range lies in the **vertical section**. Strong acid/strong base: any; strong acid/weak base: methyl orange; weak acid/strong base: phenolphthalein; weak/weak: none.

title: Titration curves
body: the equivalence pH is $7$ (SA/SB), $<7$ (SA/WB), $>7$ (WA/SB). **Half-equivalence point $=\mathrm pK_a$.**

title: $K_{sp}$ and solubility $s$
body: $\mathrm{AB}$: $K_{sp}=s^2$; $\mathrm{AB_2}$ (or $\mathrm A_2\mathrm B$): $K_{sp}=4s^3$; $\mathrm{AB_3}$: $27s^4$; $\mathrm A_2\mathrm B_3$: $108s^5$. **Precipitation** if the ionic product exceeds $K_{sp}$. **Common-ion effect:** the added ion fixes one concentration, so $s$ falls.

title: Solubility in complexing/acid
body: add $\mathrm{NH_3}$ to dissolve $\mathrm{AgCl}$ (complex ion removes $\mathrm{Ag^+}$); add acid to dissolve a hydroxide (neutralises $\mathrm{OH^-}$).

title: Distribution (partition) coefficient
body: $K_{pc}=\dfrac{[\mathrm X]_1}{[\mathrm X]_2}$ at a fixed temperature. **Several small extractions beat one large one.**

title: Ionic product of water
body: $K_w$ rises with temperature (pH of pure water is below 7 when hot but it stays neutral).

title: Acid strength vs concentration
body: a weak acid can be concentrated; a strong acid can be dilute. They are different properties.

title: Order from initial rates
body: Compare two experiments that change **one** concentration: rate ratio $=(\text{concentration ratio})^{\text{order}}$. Double $[\mathrm A]$ and rate $\times2\Rightarrow$ order 1; $\times4\Rightarrow$ order 2; no change $\Rightarrow$ order 0.

title: Units of $k$
body: overall order $n$ gives $\mathrm{mol}^{1-n}\mathrm{dm}^{3(n-1)}\mathrm s^{-1}$. First order: $\mathrm s^{-1}$; second order: $\mathrm{mol^{-1}\,dm^3\,s^{-1}}$; zero order: $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$.

title: Half-life of a first-order reaction is constant
body: $t_{1/2}=\dfrac{\ln2}k$ (not on the data booklet) $\Rightarrow$ $k=\dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}$. **If successive half-lives are equal, it is first order.** Check this on a concentration–time graph before calculating $k$.

title: Graph shapes
body: concentration vs time: straight line down (zero order), exponential decay (first order). Rate vs concentration: horizontal line (zero), straight line through the origin (first), curve (second). **The gradient of a concentration–time curve is the rate**; the initial rate is the gradient at $t=0$.

title: Rate-determining step
body: the rate equation shows the species in (or before) the slow step. **Order $=$ the number of molecules in the RDS**. A mechanism must add to the overall equation and the RDS must agree with the rate equation.

title: Arrhenius
body: $k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}$, $\ln k=\ln A-\dfrac{E_a}{RT}$. **Plot $\ln k$ against $\dfrac1T$**: gradient $=-\dfrac{E_a}R$, intercept $\ln A$. **Two temperatures:** $\ln\dfrac{k_2}{k_1}=\dfrac{E_a}R\left(\dfrac1{T_1}-\dfrac1{T_2}\right)$ — no graph needed.

title: Rule of thumb
body: for $E_a\approx50\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ near room temperature, a $10\ \mathrm K$ rise about doubles the rate.

title: Maxwell–Boltzmann
body: the curve **starts at the origin**, the area under it stays the same; at higher $T$ the peak shifts right and **lowers** and more molecules exceed $E_a$. A catalyst lowers $E_a$ so a larger shaded fraction exceeds it (the curve doesn't change).

title: Catalysis
body: heterogeneous (surface adsorption), homogeneous (intermediate), **autocatalysis**. Explain: "lowers the activation energy by providing an alternative route".

title: Clock reactions
body: rate $\propto\dfrac1t$; plot $\dfrac1t$ against concentration to get the order (a straight line through the origin means first order).

title: Reaction profile for a two-step mechanism
body: two humps with an intermediate between; the **higher** hump is the RDS.

title: Rate vs equilibrium
body: rate laws come from experiments, not from the stoichiometry (except for an elementary step).

section: 8. Periodicity, Group 2, Group 17, nitrogen and sulfur (topics 9–12)
title: Period 3 oxides
body: $\mathrm{Na_2O}$ (basic), $\mathrm{MgO}$ (basic), $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ (**amphoteric**), $\mathrm{SiO_2}$ (acidic, giant covalent), $\mathrm{P_4O_{10}}$ (acidic), $\mathrm{SO_2}/\mathrm{SO_3}$ (acidic). Melting points: giant structures high, simple molecular low.

section: 8. Periodicity, Group 2, Group 17, nitrogen and sulfur (topics 9–12)
title: Period 3 chlorides
body: $\mathrm{NaCl}$ (dissolves, neutral); $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ (slightly acidic); $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ (hydrolyses, acidic with fumes of $\mathrm{HCl}$); $\mathrm{SiCl_4}$, $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ fully hydrolysed to $\mathrm{HCl}$ and an oxo-acid (acidic, white fumes).

section: 8. Periodicity, Group 2, Group 17, nitrogen and sulfur (topics 9–12)
title: Group 2 trends down the group
body: reactivity **increases**; **hydroxide solubility increases**, **sulfate solubility decreases** (mnemonic: *"hydroxides get happy, sulfates sad"*); **thermal stability of carbonates and nitrates increases** (smaller polarising power of larger cations). **Thermal decomposition:** $\mathrm{MCO_3}\to\mathrm{MO}+\mathrm{CO_2}$; $2\mathrm{M(NO_3)_2}\to2\mathrm{MO}+4\mathrm{NO_2}+\mathrm{O_2}$ (group 1: nitrites, $2\mathrm{MNO_3}\to2\mathrm{MNO_2}+\mathrm{O_2}$, except lithium).

section: 8. Periodicity, Group 2, Group 17, nitrogen and sulfur (topics 9–12)
title: Group 2 reactions
body: with water $\mathrm M+2\mathrm{H_2O}\to\mathrm{M(OH)_2}+\mathrm{H_2}$ (Mg slow, Ba fast); oxides $+$ water $\to$ hydroxides; limewater turns milky ($\mathrm{CaCO_3}$), cloudy with $\mathrm{CO_2}$.

section: 8. Periodicity, Group 2, Group 17, nitrogen and sulfur (topics 9–12)
title: Group 17 trends down
body: **oxidising power decreases** ($\mathrm{Cl_2}>\mathrm{Br_2}>\mathrm{I_2}$); halide ion **reducing power increases** ($\mathrm{I^-}>\mathrm{Br^-}>\mathrm{Cl^-}$); boiling point rises (more electrons, stronger London forces). A halogen displaces a less reactive halide.

section: 8. Periodicity, Group 2, Group 17, nitrogen and sulfur (topics 9–12)
title: Halides + conc. $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$
body: $\mathrm{NaCl}\to\mathrm{HCl}$ only (steamy fumes); $\mathrm{NaBr}\to\mathrm{HBr}$ then $\mathrm{Br_2}$ (brown) + $\mathrm{SO_2}$; $\mathrm{NaI}\to\mathrm{I_2}$ (purple vapour/black solid), $\mathrm{SO_2}$, $\mathrm S$, **$\mathrm{H_2S}$** (smells of bad eggs). It shows the increasing reducing power.

section: 8. Periodicity, Group 2, Group 17, nitrogen and sulfur (topics 9–12)
title: Silver halide tests
body: $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$ (after adding dilute $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ to remove carbonate): $\mathrm{AgCl}$ white (dissolves in **dilute** $\mathrm{NH_3}$), $\mathrm{AgBr}$ cream (dissolves in **concentrated** $\mathrm{NH_3}$), $\mathrm{AgI}$ yellow (insoluble).

section: 8. Periodicity, Group 2, Group 17, nitrogen and sulfur (topics 9–12)
title: Disproportionation
body: $\mathrm{Cl_2}+2\mathrm{NaOH}\to\mathrm{NaCl}+\mathrm{NaClO}+\mathrm{H_2O}$ (cold, dilute); hot: $3\mathrm{Cl_2}+6\mathrm{NaOH}\to5\mathrm{NaCl}+\mathrm{NaClO_3}+3\mathrm{H_2O}$. $\mathrm{Cl_2}+\mathrm{H_2O}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{HCl}+\mathrm{HClO}$. **Same element oxidised and reduced.**

section: 8. Periodicity, Group 2, Group 17, nitrogen and sulfur (topics 9–12)
title: Hydrogen halides
body: thermal stability falls $\mathrm{HCl}>\mathrm{HBr}>\mathrm{HI}$ (longer, weaker bond).

section: 8. Periodicity, Group 2, Group 17, nitrogen and sulfur (topics 9–12)
title: Nitrogen
body: $\mathrm{N_2}$ is inert (triple bond $945\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$); $\mathrm{NH_3}$ base; $\mathrm{NH_4^+}+\mathrm{OH^-}\to\mathrm{NH_3}$ (gently warm: damp red litmus turns blue); **nitrate in soil/eutrophication**; **acid rain** from $\mathrm{SO_2}$ and $\mathrm{NO_x}$; catalytic converter $2\mathrm{CO}+2\mathrm{NO}\to2\mathrm{CO_2}+\mathrm{N_2}$.

section: 8. Periodicity, Group 2, Group 17, nitrogen and sulfur (topics 9–12)
title: Sulfur
body: contact process $\mathrm{V_2O_5}$, $450^\circ\mathrm C$, $1$–$2$ atm; **why**: compromise between yield and rate; $\mathrm{SO_3}$ is absorbed in $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ not water (fog).

section: 8. Periodicity, Group 2, Group 17, nitrogen and sulfur (topics 9–12)
title: Haber process
body: $\mathrm{Fe}$, $450^\circ\mathrm C$, $200$ atm; $\mathrm N_2+3\mathrm H_2\rightleftharpoons2\mathrm{NH_3}$ ($\Delta H<0$). **Compromise** between yield, rate and cost.

title: Count structural isomers systematically
body: vary the chain length first, then the branch position, then functional group position. For $\mathrm{C_5H_{12}}$ there are 3; for $\mathrm{C_6H_{14}}$ 5; for $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}O}$ alcohols 4.

title: Chiral centre
body: a carbon with **four different groups**; $n$ chiral centres $\to$ up to $2^n$ stereoisomers. Enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions; a **racemic mixture** has no net rotation (e.g. $\mathrm{S_N1}$ on a chiral centre, or the nucleophilic addition to a ketone).

title: E/Z (cis/trans)
body: requires a $\mathrm C{=}\mathrm C$ with **two different groups on each carbon**; use CIP priority on each carbon.

title: Degrees of unsaturation (not in syllabus, very useful)
body: $\mathrm{DBE}=\dfrac{2C+2+N-H-X}2$. $1$ means one ring or one $\mathrm{C{=}C}$ or one $\mathrm{C{=}O}$; $4$ or more suggests a benzene ring.

title: Free-radical substitution
body: **initiation** (UV breaks $\mathrm{Cl{-}Cl}$ into $\mathrm{Cl\cdot}$), **propagation** (two steps that regenerate the radical), **termination** (two radicals combine). Gives a mixture of products (further substitution), so poor yield.

title: Electrophilic addition
body: **Markovnikov** — the electrophile $\mathrm H^+$ goes to the carbon with **more** hydrogens; the more stable carbocation (tertiary $>$ secondary $>$ primary) forms the major product. $\mathrm{Br_2}$ in the dark decolourises: **bromine water test** for $\mathrm C{=}\mathrm C$.

title: Nucleophilic substitution
body: **primary** halogenoalkanes mostly $\mathrm S_N2$ (one-step, inversion, rate $=k[\mathrm{RX}][\mathrm{Nu}]$); **tertiary** mostly $\mathrm S_N1$ (carbocation intermediate, **racemic**, rate $=k[\mathrm{RX}]$); secondary: both. **Reactivity:** $\mathrm{R{-}I}>\mathrm{R{-}Br}>\mathrm{R{-}Cl}$ (weaker bond), not polarity. Test: warm with $\mathrm{AgNO_3(aq)}$ in ethanol — yellow ppt fastest for iodides.

title: Substitution vs elimination
body: **aqueous** $\mathrm{NaOH}$, warm $\to$ substitution (alcohol); **ethanolic** $\mathrm{KOH}$, heat $\to$ elimination (alkene). $\mathrm{KCN}$ in ethanol gives a nitrile (**adds a carbon**); $\mathrm{NH_3}$ in excess ethanol under pressure gives a primary amine.

title: Oxidation of alcohols
body: **primary** $\to$ aldehyde (**distil** as it forms) $\to$ carboxylic acid (**reflux** with excess oxidant); **secondary** $\to$ ketone; **tertiary** — no reaction. Acidified $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}$: orange $\to$ green. $\mathrm{[O]}$ shorthand is fine for the equation if allowed.

title: Reductions
body: $\mathrm{LiAlH_4}$ (dry ether) reduces aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, amides, nitriles; $\mathrm{NaBH_4}$ reduces **only aldehydes and ketones**. Catalytic hydrogenation ($\mathrm{H_2}$/Ni) reduces $\mathrm{C{=}C}$ and also aldehydes/ketones.

title: Carbonyl tests
body: **2,4-DNPH** — orange ppt for aldehydes and ketones (melting point of the ppt identifies the compound); **Tollens'** — silver mirror (aldehydes only); **Fehling's/Benedict's** — brick-red ppt (aldehydes only). **Iodoform** ($\mathrm{I_2}$/NaOH): yellow ppt for $\mathrm{CH_3C{=}O}$ or $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)}$ groups.

title: Nucleophilic addition to carbonyl
body: $\mathrm{HCN}$ + trace base gives a hydroxynitrile (adds a carbon; racemic from planar $\mathrm{C{=}O}$); aldehydes more reactive than ketones (less steric hindrance, more $\delta+$).

title: Carboxylic acids
body: **acid tests** — effervescence with $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ ($\mathrm{CO_2}$); **esterification** acid + alcohol, conc. $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ catalyst, reflux (reversible); **acid chloride** with $\mathrm{SOCl_2}$/$\mathrm{PCl_5}$ — much more reactive route to esters/amides. **Hydrolysis of esters:** acid (reversible) or alkali (irreversible, gives carboxylate salt).

title: Amines and amides
body: amines are bases (lone pair on N): $\mathrm{R{-}NH_2}$ stronger base than ammonia (alkyl groups push electrons) and aniline weaker (lone pair delocalised). Amides: neutral. Amide hydrolysis needs heat.

title: Phenol
body: **more** acidic than alcohols (weaker than carboxylic acids): reacts with $\mathrm{NaOH}$ but **not** $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$; bromine water gives a **white precipitate** (2,4,6-tribromophenol) at room temperature without a catalyst; neutral $\mathrm{FeCl_3}$ gives **violet**.

title: Benzene
body: **electrophilic substitution** (not addition) because delocalised $\pi$ electrons are stable. Nitration: conc. $\mathrm{HNO_3}$/conc. $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, $<55^\circ\mathrm C$ (higher gives dinitro); halogenation: $\mathrm{Br_2}$ with $\mathrm{FeBr_3}$ or $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$; Friedel–Crafts alkylation: $\mathrm{RCl}$/$\mathrm{AlCl_3}$; acylation $\mathrm{RCOCl}$/$\mathrm{AlCl_3}$. **Directing effects:** $\mathrm{OH}$, $\mathrm{NH_2}$, alkyl are **2,4-directing and activating**; $\mathrm{NO_2}$, $\mathrm{COOH}$, $\mathrm{CHO}$ are **3-directing and deactivating**.

title: Benzene stability evidence
body: all $\mathrm{C{-}C}$ bonds are $0.140\ \mathrm{nm}$; hydrogenation enthalpy is less exothermic than three times that of cyclohexene (about $150\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ extra stability).

title: Polymers
body: **addition** — remove the double bond, show **two bonds extending** from the repeat unit (e.g. $\left[-\mathrm{CH_2{-}CH(Cl)-}\right]_n$). **Condensation** — polyester (diol + diacid, loses $\mathrm{H_2O}$) or polyamide (diamine + diacid, or amino acid); **find the monomers by breaking the ester/amide link and adding back $\mathrm{OH}$/$\mathrm H$**. Condensation polymers are **hydrolysable**; addition polymers are not (non-biodegradable).

title: Amino acids and peptides
body: zwitterion $\mathrm{H_3N^+{-}CHR{-}COO^-}$ at the isoelectric point; in acid the $\mathrm{COO^-}$ is protonated (**cation**), in alkali the $\mathrm{NH_3^+}$ loses a proton (**anion**), so they migrate in electrophoresis. Hydrolysis of a peptide gives the amino acids.

title: Synthesis route planning
body: **work backwards** from the target; know the interconversions: alkane $\to$ halogenoalkane (radical) $\to$ alcohol/nitrile/amine ($\mathrm{S_N}$) $\to$ aldehyde/ketone/acid (oxidation) $\to$ ester/amide; alkene $\leftrightarrow$ alcohol, alkene $\to$ halogenoalkane. **Each step: reagent, conditions and name of the reaction.**

title: Safe and standard apparatus
body: reflux (prevents loss of volatile reagents), distillation (separates by boiling point), **drying with anhydrous $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ or $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$**, separating funnel.

title: Chromatography
body: $R_f=\dfrac{\text{distance moved by spot}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}}$; compare with standards.

title: IR absorptions to know
body: (wavenumber, $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$): $\mathrm{O{-}H}$ alcohol $3200$–$3600$ (broad); $\mathrm{O{-}H}$ carboxylic acid $2500$–$3300$ (very broad, overlaps $\mathrm{C{-}H}$); $\mathrm{N{-}H}$ $3300$–$3500$; $\mathrm{C{-}H}$ $2850$–$3100$; $\mathrm{C{\equiv}N}$ $2200$–$2260$; **$\mathrm{C{=}O}$ $1680$–$1750$** (strong, sharp); $\mathrm{C{=}C}$ $1620$–$1680$; $\mathrm{C{-}O}$ $1000$–$1300$. Match the pattern of peaks, not a single one.

title: Mass spectrum fragments
body: **M** peak gives $M_r$; common fragments **$15$ ($\mathrm{CH_3}^+$), $29$ ($\mathrm{C_2H_5}^+$ or $\mathrm{CHO}^+$), $43$ ($\mathrm{C_3H_7}^+$ or $\mathrm{CH_3CO}^+$), $45$ ($\mathrm{COOH}^+$ or $\mathrm{OC_2H_5}^+$), $77$ ($\mathrm{C_6H_5}^+$)**. Loss of $18$ is water; loss of $17$ is $\mathrm{OH}$; loss of $15$ is $\mathrm{CH_3}$. The **base peak** is the tallest, not necessarily M.

title: $^{13}$C NMR
body: **number of peaks $=$ number of different carbon environments** (use symmetry). Shifts: alkyl $0$–$50$, $\mathrm{C{-}O}$ $50$–$90$, $\mathrm{C{=}C}$ / aromatic $100$–$150$, $\mathrm{C{=}O}$ $160$–$220$.

title: $^1$H NMR
body: **peaks $=$ environments; integration (area) $=$ ratio of H; splitting: $n+1$ rule** (a peak is split into $n+1$ lines by $n$ neighbouring H on adjacent carbons). **Shifts ($\delta$):** alkyl $0.9$–$1.7$; next to $\mathrm{C{=}O}$ $2.0$–$2.7$; $\mathrm{O{-}CH}$ $3.3$–$4.3$; $\mathrm{C{=}C{-}H}$ $4.5$–$6$; aromatic $6.5$–$8$; aldehyde $9.4$–$10$; $\mathrm{COOH}$ $10$–$12$; $\mathrm{OH}/\mathrm{NH}$ variable. **$\mathrm D_2\mathrm O$ shake removes the $\mathrm{OH}$ and $\mathrm{NH}$ peaks.** Reference: **TMS** at $0$ ppm.

title: Solve an unknown structure
body: (1) $M_r$ and formula (or DBE) $\to$ (2) IR for functional groups $\to$ (3) $^{13}$C count (symmetry) $\to$ (4) $^1$H integration and splitting $\to$ (5) fit fragments in the mass spectrum. Draw it and check each piece.

title: Combined integration ratios
body: the integration gives the **simplest ratio**; multiply to match the molecular formula's total H.

title: Gas–liquid chromatography
body: retention time identifies; peak area gives amount.

title: Cation tests with $\mathrm{NaOH}$ (and excess)
body: $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ white ppt, **insoluble in excess**; $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ white ppt (slight); $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ white ppt **soluble in excess** (amphoteric); $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ white ppt soluble in excess (also in ammonia); $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ **pale blue** ppt, insoluble in excess $\mathrm{NaOH}$ but gives a **deep blue solution in excess $\mathrm{NH_3}$**; $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ **green** ppt (turns brown on standing); $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ **red-brown** ppt; $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ **green** ppt, soluble in excess (green solution); $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ off-white ppt, browning in air.

title: Anion tests
body: $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$: dilute acid $\to$ $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (limewater milky); $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$: $\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}$ (after acid) $\to$ white ppt; $\mathrm{Cl^-},\mathrm{Br^-},\mathrm{I^-}$: see above; $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$: warm with $\mathrm{NaOH}$ and aluminium foil $\to$ $\mathrm{NH_3}$; $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$: warm with $\mathrm{NaOH}$ $\to$ $\mathrm{NH_3}$ (red litmus blue).

title: Gas tests
body: $\mathrm{H_2}$ — squeaky pop; $\mathrm{O_2}$ — relights a glowing splint; $\mathrm{CO_2}$ — limewater milky; $\mathrm{NH_3}$ — damp red litmus blue; $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ — damp blue litmus red then bleaches; $\mathrm{SO_2}$ — acidified dichromate orange to green; $\mathrm{HCl}$ — white fumes with $\mathrm{NH_3}$.

title: Transition elements
body: **variable oxidation states**, **coloured compounds** (d–d transitions, colour depends on the ligand and oxidation state), **catalysts**, **complex ions**. Colours: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ blue, $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ pale green, $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ yellow-brown, $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ pale pink, $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ green, $\mathrm{Co^{2+}}$ pink, $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}$ orange, $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ purple.

title: Ligand exchange
body: $\mathrm{[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}\to[\mathrm{Cu(NH_3)_4(H_2O)_2}]^{2+}$ (deep blue); $\to[\mathrm{CuCl_4}]^{2-}$ (yellow-green) with conc. $\mathrm{HCl}$. **Co-ordination number:** 6 octahedral, 4 tetrahedral or square planar, 2 linear ($\mathrm{[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+}$). Charge of the complex $=$ metal charge $+$ ligand charges.

title: Colour from $\Delta E$
body: the complex absorbs one colour and shows the complement; $\Delta E=hf$.

title: Redox titrations
body: $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}:\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}=1:5$; $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}:\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}=2:5$; $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}:\mathrm{H_2O_2}=2:5$; $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}:\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}=1:6$; $\mathrm{I_2}:\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2-}}=1:2$. **Iodine–thiosulfate:** add starch near the end (blue-black $\to$ colourless). **Endpoint of permanganate:** first permanent faint pink.

title: Ligand substitution and stability
body: bidentate ligands (**edta**, en) give **more stable** complexes (entropy gain from releasing more small molecules).

title: Haemoglobin / Cisplatin facts
body: $\mathrm{CO}$ binds more strongly to $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ than $\mathrm{O_2}$ (toxic); cisplatin binds to DNA (square planar $\mathrm{Pt(II)}$).

title: Reading a burette
body: to $\pm0.05\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, give to 2 d.p. (ending in 0 or 5). Percentage error $=\dfrac{\text{uncertainty}}{\text{reading}}\times100$; for a titre, **two readings** so double the burette uncertainty.

title: Reduce uncertainty
body: use a larger amount, a more precise apparatus, repeat and average.

title: Planning and evaluation
body: state the **independent**, **dependent** and **control** variables; give a safe method with quantities; **at least five values** in a range; repeat; draw the graph with a line of best fit.

title: Graph to constant
body: rearrange to $y=mx+c$ first, then read the gradient with a big triangle.

title: Common errors in "improvements"
body: avoid "be more careful" or "human error"; instead name a specific change (use a gas syringe instead of an inverted cylinder, insulate the calorimeter, use a pipette instead of a measuring cylinder).

title: Carry a named quantity through the chain
body: When a calculation has several stages, label each intermediate as a species and location, such as $n(\mathrm{HCl\ in\ titre})$ or $n(\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}\ in\ flask})$, before substituting numbers. At the end, check that the requested answer refers to the same substance and sample size, rather than an intermediate $M_r$ or an aliquot amount.

title: Use an answer bound before calculating
body: Before a long calculation, write a chemical bound: percentage yield $\leq100\%$, a component's partial pressure $<P_{\mathrm{total}}$, or reacted moles $\leq$ initial moles. A result outside that bound usually locates a reversed ratio, wrong sample volume or unit conversion before you redo every line.

title: Keep the aliquot fraction visible
body: If a stock solution of volume $V_s$ supplies an aliquot $V_a$, write $n_{\mathrm{stock}}=n_{\mathrm{aliquot}}(V_s/V_a)$ on its own line; this prevents a factor-of-ten error when the reaction ratio also differs from $1:1$. Check that $V_s/V_a>1$ and that the total stock amount exceeds the aliquot amount.

title: Back-titration subtraction line
body: When an excess reagent is added and its remainder is titrated, write $n_{\mathrm{reacted}}=n_{\mathrm{added}}-n_{\mathrm{remaining}}$ before applying any coefficient or aliquot factor. Check that the remainder is less than the initial amount and that the calculated amount of analyte is positive.

title: Mass-loss ledger for heating
body: For a decomposition experiment, write three separate differences: $m_{\mathrm{sample}}=m_{\mathrm{vessel+sample}}-m_{\mathrm{vessel}}$, $m_{\mathrm{residue}}=m_{\mathrm{vessel+residue}}-m_{\mathrm{vessel}}$, and $m_{\mathrm{lost}}=m_{\mathrm{sample}}-m_{\mathrm{residue}}$. Use $m_{\mathrm{lost}}$ for moles of gas only when the stated reaction and conditions show that the lost mass is that gas; check $0<m_{\mathrm{lost}}<m_{\mathrm{sample}}$.

title: Balance unfamiliar equations in a fixed order
body: When a product is supplied but the full equation is not, balance the least common element first, then metals or other non-H/O atoms, then oxygen with $\mathrm{H_2O}$ if aqueous conditions permit, and hydrogen last. Recount every element and charge after the last coefficient; the examiner used this sequence for $\mathrm{Al_4C_3}$ reacting with alkali.

title: Neutralisation first, equilibrium second
body: When strong acid or base is mixed with a weak acid, weak base or its salt, calculate $n(\mathrm{H^+})-n(\mathrm{OH^-})$ and the surviving amounts before choosing a pH equation. Check whether both conjugate partners remain (buffer), one weak species remains, or strong reagent is in excess.

title: Isotopologue masses by pair sums
body: For a diatomic molecule made from isotopes, list every unordered isotope pair, including mixed pairs, then add the two mass numbers and merge pairs with the same total. This catches low-abundance middle peaks such as $^{16}\mathrm O{}^{17}\mathrm O$ and $^{17}\mathrm O{}^{18}\mathrm O$; check the smallest and largest possible totals first.

title: Compare similar molecules by holding one force fixed
body: If two small molecules have equal or nearly equal electron counts and comparable shapes, treat their London forces as roughly similar, then compare permanent dipoles to decide a boiling-point ordering. Check that the species really are comparable in size and shape before using this shortcut.

title: Dry-gas pressure over water
body: If a gas is collected over water and water-vapour pressure is given, use $p_{\mathrm{dry}}=p_{\mathrm{total}}-p_{\mathrm{H_2O}}$ in $pV=nRT$. Check that $p_{\mathrm{dry}}<p_{\mathrm{total}}$; using total pressure would overestimate the gas moles.

title: Read $\Delta S$ from a Gibbs plot
body: For a straight plot of $\Delta G$ against $T$ under conditions where $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ are approximately constant, $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S$ gives gradient $=-\Delta S$ and intercept $=\Delta H$. Check the axis units before reporting $\Delta S$, especially if $\Delta G$ is in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

title: Potential is intensive
body: When balancing half-equations, multiply electron and species coefficients but never multiply the tabulated $E^\circ$ values; calculate $E^\circ_{\mathrm{cell}}$ from the two unchanged reduction potentials. A doubled overall equation must give the same $E^\circ_{\mathrm{cell}}$, which is a quick check on the working.

title: Check disproportionation with two reduction potentials
body: If the same intermediate oxidation state can be reduced and oxidised, pair its reduction half-equation with the reverse of its oxidation partner and calculate $E^\circ_{\mathrm{cell}}=E^\circ_{\mathrm{reduction}}-E^\circ_{\mathrm{reversed\ pair}}$. A positive value predicts thermodynamic feasibility under the stated standard conditions; check that the balanced sum really consumes the intermediate on both sides.

title: Cancel a common total pressure
body: For a gas equilibrium with $\Delta n_{\mathrm{gas}}=0$, substitute $p_i=x_iP$ into $K_p$ and cancel $P$ before inserting numbers. The result depends only on equilibrium mole fractions, so changing total pressure alone cannot change $K_p$ or the equilibrium composition of an ideal-gas mixture at fixed temperature.

title: Inert gas: name the constraint
body: Adding inert gas at constant volume and temperature leaves each reacting gas's $p_i=n_iRT/V$ unchanged, so there is no immediate equilibrium shift; at constant total pressure, volume grows and reacting partial pressures fall. For the constant-pressure case, use the change in gas moles to predict the direction, and check whether the question specifies volume or pressure.

title: Use stoichiometric symmetry before algebra
body: If an equilibrium forms $\mathrm H_2$ and $\mathrm I_2$ in a $1:1$ ratio from only $\mathrm{HI}$, set their equilibrium amounts equal immediately and obtain the remaining $p_{\mathrm{HI}}$ by subtraction from total pressure. Check that the two product partial pressures match before calculating $K_p$.

title: Common-ion solubility check
body: For $\mathrm{MX(s)}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{M^+(aq)}+\mathrm{X^-(aq)}$ in a solution already containing $c$ of $\mathrm X^-$, estimate $s\approx K_{sp}/c$ only if $s\ll c$. Test that inequality with the computed $s$; otherwise solve $s(c+s)=K_{sp}$.

title: Exact weak-acid root when the approximation fails
body: For a monoprotic acid initially at concentration $c$ with negligible water contribution, put $x=[\mathrm H^+]$ and solve $x^2+K_ax-K_ac=0$, giving $x=(\sqrt{K_a^2+4K_ac}-K_a)/2$. Use it when the approximate result $\sqrt{K_ac}$ is not small relative to $c$; check $0<x<c$.

title: Dilution direction check for weak acids
body: A dilution by factor $d$ raises a weak monoprotic acid's pH by approximately $\tfrac12\log_{10}d$ only while $[\mathrm H^+]\ll c$ and water ionisation is negligible. Thus a tenfold dilution gives about $0.5$ pH unit, providing a quick check against treating the acid as fully dissociated.

title: Use rate ratios to remove $k$
body: When two experiments change several reactant concentrations at once, divide their rate laws so that $k$ cancels, then insert already known orders to solve the remaining order. Check by predicting one measured rate from a different row of the table.

title: Decimal-log Arrhenius slope
body: If the plotted axis is explicitly $\log_{10}k$ against $1/T$, the gradient is $-E_a/(2.303R)$; the familiar $-E_a/R$ applies to $\ln k$. Check the actual axis label and any equation supplied in the question before converting the gradient to $E_a$.

title: Logarithmic first-order interval
body: If first-order behaviour is established and two concentrations are known at times $t_1,t_2$, use $k=\ln(c_1/c_2)/(t_2-t_1)$ without needing a half-life or a plotted tangent. Check that $c_2<c_1$ for a disappearing reactant and that $k$ is positive with units of inverse time.

title: Rate units inherit the clock
body: Derive $k$ units from the rate unit printed in the question, including its actual time unit: a first-order rate in $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}\,min^{-1}}$ gives $k$ in $\mathrm{min^{-1}}$. Check that the time unit in your final $k$ matches the time unit used in the data or graph.

section: 8. Periodicity, Group 2, Group 17, nitrogen and sulfur (topics 9–12)
title: Use the comparison that cancels a common cause
body: In a periodicity explanation involving two species, first identify what is held nearly fixed (shell count, electron count or structure), then name the changing quantity (nuclear charge, shielding or bond strength). This keeps the explanation tied to the actual comparison; check that the chosen fixed property really is shared by both species.

title: Inventory every functional group before choosing a reagent
body: For a molecule with several groups, mark each site that the proposed reagent could attack and write all resulting changes before matching a product or test. For example, an oxidant may convert an aldehyde and a secondary alcohol in the same molecule; check that no unreacted group in your product should also have changed.

title: Count ester choices by the carbon split
body: For an acyclic ester with $N$ total carbons, enumerate acid-side and alcohol-side carbon counts as $(1,N-1),(2,N-2),\ldots,(N-1,1)$, then list branch isomers within each split. Check that the carbonyl carbon stays on the acid side and that each drawn structure has exactly $N$ carbons.

title: Collapse symmetric stereoisomers
body: After assigning E/Z at two double bonds or configurations at equivalent sites, rotate or reflect the whole molecule before counting a second structure as new. If a symmetric molecule makes $(E,Z)$ identical to $(Z,E)$, count that pair once; check the equivalence on drawn structures rather than labels alone.

title: Check an ester or amide backwards by its bond
body: For a proposed condensation product, split the $\mathrm{C(=O){-}O}$ or $\mathrm{C(=O){-}N}$ bond and restore $\mathrm{OH}$ to the acyl fragment and H to the O/N fragment to identify possible reactants. Then recombine them and check that the product's carbon skeleton and number of links match the question.

title: Oxidative cleavage by carbon fate
body: For hot, concentrated acidified $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ cleavage of an alkene, mark each alkene carbon: a carbon bearing H can become a carboxylic acid, while a carbon with no H can become a ketone; a terminal $\mathrm{CH_2}$ can be oxidised further to $\mathrm{CO_2}$. Cut each $\mathrm{C{=}C}$ only once and check the carbon count across all products.

title: Addition stoichiometry counts multiple bonds
body: For complete addition of bromine to isolated carbon–carbon double bonds, one mole of $\mathrm{Br_2}$ reacts per mole of $\mathrm{C{=}C}$, so $n(\mathrm{Br_2})/n(\mathrm{molecule})$ can reveal the number of double bonds. Check that the reaction specified is addition and that other groups do not also consume bromine under those conditions.

title: Use isotope spacing to infer charge
body: In an isotope cluster, adjacent isotopic mass differences appear $1/z$ units apart on the $m/z$ axis for ion charge $z$; a 2-unit mass difference therefore appears 1 unit apart for a $2+$ ion. Check the proposed charge against the ion formula and the full cluster before assigning a peak.

title: Balance complex-ion equations as a ligand ledger
body: In ligand substitution, write the complete coordination spheres first, then place displaced ligands on the other side and balance any incoming ligands, water and charge. Check separately that metal atoms, ligand atoms and total charge match; a colour change alone does not determine coefficients.

title: Acidify before testing a hydrolysed halide
body: If a halogenoalkane was heated with excess aqueous $\mathrm{NaOH}$, acidify the sample with dilute $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ before adding $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$, otherwise residual $\mathrm{OH^-}$ can interfere. Confirm the halide from precipitate colour and ammonia solubility, then check that the organic hydrolysis product no longer contains halogen.

title: Put units in table headings once
source: examiner report 9701 s23 pp19,22; mark scheme 9701 s24 paper 33 p6
body: Before collecting readings, make a column for each raw measurement and put its unit in the heading, for example $V/\mathrm{cm^3}$ or $t/\mathrm s$; keep all entries in a column at instrument-appropriate precision. Check that calculated columns, such as titre, have their own heading and are not confused with raw readings.

title: Follow the stated instrument resolution
body: Record a thermometer marked in $1\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$ steps to the nearest $0.5\,^{\circ}\mathrm C$ when that is the allowed interpolation, and a coarse measuring cylinder to its actual readable division rather than invented decimal places. Check the apparatus scale before deciding precision; extra zeros do not make a measurement more accurate.

title: Make the graph use its space
body: Choose linear axis scales that spread the measured points over most of the grid, and draw a curve when the plotted trend curves rather than forcing a straight line. Check any requested intersection by projecting it carefully to both labelled scales and reporting the precision supported by the graph.

title: Read a gradient from the fitted line
body: Choose two well-separated points on the line of best fit, not necessarily original data points, and calculate $\Delta y/\Delta x$ with both axis scale factors. Check the gradient's units as $[y]/[x]$ and its sign against the plotted slope.

title: Trace systematic error through a formula
body: For an evaluation question, change the measured quantity first, then propagate that direction through each equation before stating whether the final answer rises or falls. For example, spilled residue makes measured mass loss too large, but the effect on a calculated $A_r$ must be determined from the actual subsequent formula.

title: Name the observable event exactly
body: In qualitative analysis, distinguish a precipitate formed when solutions are mixed from a solid reagent that remains undissolved, and reserve “decolourised” for a solution becoming colourless. Check that the written observation describes a change seen in the tube, rather than merely naming the reagent's initial colour.

title: Use the question's allowed test set
body: When asked to distinguish two unknowns with one test, choose a reagent that gives different observations and state both expected outcomes, then stop. Check any instruction forbidding further tests; an extra speculative test can contradict the identification.
